hints: Think about what makes benzene especially stable and what would be lost if Br atoms added across the ring.
walkthrough:
Picture what addition would do**
Imagine $\text{Br}_2$ adding across one of the bonds in benzene like it does with an alkene. You would break the continuous ring of p-orbitals. The product would no longer be a flat ring with 6 delocalised pi-electrons.

Link stability to substitution**
Benzene is extra stable because of that delocalised aromatic system. Substitution replaces one $\text{H}$ with $\text{Br}$ but leaves the delocalised ring intact in the final product, so it keeps that stabilisation. Addition loses it, so it does not happen.
Final answer: Substitution preserves the aromatic ring with delocalised 6 pi-electrons, whereas addition would destroy the delocalisation and aromatic stability.

hints: Start with the electron rich benzene pi cloud attacking the strong electrophile $\text{Br}^+$.
Recall the intermediate has one $sp^3$ carbon carrying both Br and H, with the positive charge spread around the rest of the ring.
Think how aromaticity is restored by removing the ring proton, not bromide.
walkthrough:
First attack to make the intermediate**
You have an electron rich benzene ring and a very electron poor $\text{Br}^+$. Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the benzene circle, or from a $\text{C=C}$ bond, pointing to the $\text{Br}^+$. This forms a new $\text{C-Br}$ bond and breaks aromaticity temporarily.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
One carbon is now tetrahedral, bonded to both the original $\text{H}$ and the new $\text{Br}$. The positive charge is not stuck on that carbon, it is delocalised over the other five carbons of the ring. Show the + in the ring with two remaining double bonds, or with three resonance forms.

Restore aromaticity**
Now draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond on that same tetrahedral carbon back into the ring to reform the delocalised system. $\text{H}^+$ is expelled and you get $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$. That loss of $\text{H}^+$ is what makes it substitution, not addition.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi-system to $\text{Br}^+$ to form arenium ion with Br and H on same tetrahedral carbon and + charge delocalised in ring. Curly arrow from C-H bond to reform aromatic ring, losing $\text{H}^+$ to give bromobenzene.

hints: Remember $\text{AlBr}_3 + \text{Br}_2$ gave $\text{Br}^+ + \text{AlBr}_4^-$, so look for what $\text{AlBr}_4^-$ must pick up to return $\text{AlBr}_3$.
walkthrough:
Balance the catalyst cycle**
In the first step $\text{AlBr}_3$ accepted $\text{Br}^-$ to become $\text{AlBr}_4^-$. To get back to $\text{AlBr}_3$ it must lose that bromide as part of a small molecule. The $\text{H}^+$ lost from the ring in (a)(ii) does exactly that: $$\text{AlBr}_4^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{AlBr}_3 + \text{HBr}$$ This shows $\text{AlBr}_3$ is a true catalyst.

hints: Focus on the oxygen lone pair in $\text{-OH}$ and where it can overlap with the benzene pi system.
Consider how increased electron density in the ring affects attack on $\text{Br}_2$ without a catalyst.
walkthrough:
See the activating group**
In phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, the oxygen has a lone pair in a p-orbital that overlaps with the ring pi system. That lone pair is donated partly into the ring.

Connect to reactivity with bromine**
This pushes extra electron density into the ring, especially at the 2, 4 and 6 positions. The ring is now electron rich enough to distort the electron cloud of a neutral $\text{Br}_2$ molecule and create its own $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ electrophile. So bromination is much faster and needs no $\text{AlBr}_3$.

Final answer: Lone pair on O of phenol is delocalised into the ring, increasing ring electron density. This allows phenol to polarise / induce a dipole in $\text{Br}_2$ so no $\text{AlBr}_3$ catalyst is needed.

hints: Count carbons: you need all distinct skeletons with 4 carbons carrying one + charge, structure 1 is the straight chain primary ion.
Think of the branched chain: where can the + sit on a 3 carbon chain with a methyl branch.
Remember the most stable $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9^+$ is tertiary with three methyl groups on the $\text{C}^+$.
walkthrough:
List the carbon skeletons for C4**
There are only two skeletons: straight $\text{C-C-C-C}$ and branched $\text{C-C(C)-C}$. Structure 1 given is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$, the primary straight chain ion.

Find the other straight chain ion**
On the straight chain you can also put the + on carbon 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_3$, sec-butyl cation. That is a different carbocation with the same formula.

Find the two branched ions**
On the branched skeleton $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_3$, removing H from a terminal carbon gives the primary ion $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2^+$, and removing H from the central carbon gives the tertiary ion $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$. Those complete the set of four.
Final answer: Structure 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}^+\text{CH}_3$ ; Structure 3: $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2^+$ ; Structure 4: $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{C}^+$ in any order.

hints: Each carbocation attaches through its $\text{C}^+$ carbon to the benzene ring to give a $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{14}$ isomer.
Use symmetry: tert-butylbenzene has three identical methyl carbons, so it shows the fewest peaks.
Compare n-butylbenzene (8 peaks given) with sec-butylbenzene which also has no symmetry in the side chain.
The remaining isobutylbenzene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ has two equivalent methyls, giving an intermediate peak count.
walkthrough:
Attach each cation to benzene**
Friedel-Crafts alkylation simply joins the $\text{C}^+$ to the ring with loss of $\text{H}^+$. So $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2^+$ gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (given, 8 peaks). Similarly you get $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$ and $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$.

Count environments for the most symmetric isomer**
Look at $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$. The monosubstituted ring gives 4 distinct ring carbons. The quaternary side chain carbon is 1 type, and all three methyls are equivalent, 1 type. Total $4 + 2 = 6$ peaks. This must be the 6 peak spectrum.

Count for the isobutyl isomer**
For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$, ring gives 4 types, plus $\text{CH}_2$ (1), plus $\text{CH}$ (1), plus two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups (1). Total $4 + 3 = 7$ peaks. This matches the 7 peak spectrum.

Assign the sec-butyl isomer**
For $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, ring gives 4 types and all four side chain carbons are all different: $\text{CH}$, $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$ on the branch, $\text{CH}_3$ on the end. Total $4 + 4 = 8$ peaks. This matches the second 8 peak spectrum, like n-butylbenzene which also has no equivalent side chain carbons.

Final answer: 6 peaks: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{C(CH}_3\text{)}_3$, tert-butylbenzene; 7 peaks: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)}_2$, 2-methyl-1-phenylpropane (isobutylbenzene); 8 peaks: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, 2-phenylbutane (sec-butylbenzene).
